summary: Provides a framework and requirements for using GMPLS to control flexi-grid DWDM networks, where ITU-T allows variable-width frequency slots for optical channels.

plainLanguage.summary: Fiber light used to be sliced into equal-sized lanes. Now lane widths can vary, and this explains the control needed for that.

questions: how does gmpls control flexi-grid networks
how does gmpls control flexible optical networks
what is spectrum assignment in optical networks
subtitle: Extending GMPLS to control optical networks with flexible frequency allocation.

tldr.problem: Modern high-speed optical networks need flexible allocation of spectrum rather than fixed-width channels, but existing GMPLS control protocols were designed for fixed-grid wavelength switching.
tldr.mechanism: This framework extends GMPLS concepts to flexi-grid networks where channels can have variable-sized frequency slots, defining how control plane protocols should handle spectrum assignment, routing, and resource discovery.
tldr.outcome: Enables operators to use GMPLS to control next-generation flexible optical networks, allowing efficient use of spectrum through variable-width allocation.

today: RFC 7698 is an Informational RFC published in November 2015 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the foundational framework document for GMPLS control of flexi-grid networks. Related protocol specifications for implementing this framework were published separately, including RFCs for OSPF and IS-IS extensions to carry flexi-grid information.

sections.title: Introduction to Flexi-Grid Networks
sections.content:
RFC 7698 defines a framework for controlling flexi-grid DWDM networks using GMPLS. Unlike traditional fixed-grid networks where optical channels occupy fixed 50 GHz slots, flexi-grid networks use variable-width frequency slots, allowing more flexible allocation of optical spectrum.

A frequency slot is the fundamental concept: it is a variable-sized optical frequency range assigned to a data connection, defined by its nominal central frequency and its width. The frequency grid uses 6.25 GHz granularity for center frequencies and 12.5 GHz granularity for slot width, allowing fine-grained spectrum management.

This framework applies GMPLS architectural and control-plane concepts to flexi-grid systems, termed Spectrum-Switched Optical Networks (SSON).
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of locking channels to fixed-size slots on the fiber, flexible grids let you choose any size you need. This document explains how the network control system makes these choices.

sections.title: Core Concepts of Flexi-Grid Architecture
sections.content:
Flexi-grid networks follow ITU-T layered architecture with a media layer (where spectrum switching happens) and a signal layer (where optical signals are carried). A media channel is a frequency slot with associated network path, characterized by its effective frequency slot.

Network media channels carry individual optical tributary signals (OTSi). Multiple network media channels can be grouped into a composite media channel, allowing several OTSi to be transported over a single fiber with potentially non-contiguous frequency slots.

The media layer hierarchy includes frequency slots at different points along the path. Each link may have different characteristics due to filters and amplifiers, creating effective frequency slots that represent the usable spectrum at each hop.

GMPLS represents media channels as Label Switched Paths (LSPs), where the label encodes the frequency slot parameters (central frequency and width). Unlike fixed-grid networks, these parameters can vary at each hop.
sections.plainLanguage: The network is organized in layers: the media layer switches frequency slots (light frequencies) between connections, and the signal layer carries the actual data. Signals travel through multiple hops, and each hop may adjust the slot width slightly.

sections.title: Control-Plane Requirements for Flexi-Grid
sections.content:
The control plane must support Routing and Spectrum Assignment (RSA), which determines both the path and the frequency slot for each connection. RSA can follow several architectural models:

Combined RSA (R&SA): A central entity computes both route and spectrum assignment with full network knowledge. Separated RSA (R+SA): Different entities handle routing and spectrum assignment sequentially. Routing and Distributed Spectrum Assignment (R+DSA): Routing is centralized but spectrum is assigned hop-by-hop along the path.

Signaling must be able to configure the nominal central frequency and support flexible slot widths from 12.5 GHz up to the entire C-band. The control plane must collect local frequency slots assigned at each link and support resizing of established media channels.

Routing protocols must advertise available frequency ranges and available slot-width ranges on each link, enabling path computation for any RSA model. This information exchange must support damping and thresholds to mitigate security issues from network variations.
sections.plainLanguage: The control system needs to decide which path to send light down and what frequency slot to use. It can make all decisions centrally, or split the decisions between a path planner and frequency selector, or spread the frequency selection across each network hop.

sections.title: Spectrum Assignment and Resource Allocation
sections.content:
A key challenge in flexi-grid systems is managing spectrum continuity constraints: without frequency converters, the effective frequency slot must remain valid end-to-end. The framework identifies four modes for handling spectrum parameter continuity:

Mode a: Both the center frequency (n) and width (m) can change at each hop, but the effective slot remains valid. Mode b: Width can change but center frequency stays constant. Mode c: Both parameters stay constant (simplest but most restrictive). Mode d: Center frequency can change but width stays constant.

The framework introduces Media Channel Matrices for flexible spectrum switching and discusses spectrum fragmentation—the fragmentation of available spectrum into non-contiguous ranges. Link properties must be correlated at both ends to ensure interworking, particularly when flexi-grid nodes interact with fixed-grid nodes or flexi-grid nodes with different capabilities.

Neighbor discovery and link property correlation mechanisms MUST support both out-of-band and out-of-fiber control channels to enable plug-and-play deployment where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: When light travels from one switch to another, the slot might need to stay the same width (to avoid complex conversion hardware) or the center frequency might need to stay the same. The system needs to handle these constraints so the path works end-to-end.

sections.title: Management and Implementation
sections.content:
The framework notes that GMPLS management infrastructure exists through MIB modules (RFC 4802, 4803) and emerging YANG models, but these need extensions to represent bandwidth, frequency slots, and effective frequency slots. Protocol extensions like those in RFC 4783 can report control-plane faults, and RSVP-TE messages already provide error detection mechanisms (PathErr, Notify).

The Link Management Protocol (LMP) is particularly applicable to optical networks for confirming configuration and capabilities at link endpoints. For flexi-grid networks, LMP could be extended to collect and report information about grid properties, available frequency ranges, and slot-width capabilities between link endpoints.

Data-plane Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) for optical systems is outside IETF scope but RFC 7260 provides a framework that can be applied with minor extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Managing these networks requires tools to discover what each switch can do, coordinate settings across links, and handle failures. The document explains how existing management protocols can be extended for flexible grids.
